title: What is an Adverb?
content: An adverb is a word that modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb. It can describe how, when, where, how often, or to what extent something happens. Examples: 'She sings beautifully' (how), 'Yesterday I finished my homework' (when), 'Come here!' (where).

title: What Do Adverbs Modify?
content: Adverbs modify three things: (1) Verbs — show how an action happens: 'She sings beautifully.' (2) Adjectives — modify intensity: 'The water is extremely cold.' (3) Other adverbs — strengthen or weaken meaning: 'He ran very quickly.'

title: Types of Adverbs
content: Adverbs fall into five categories: (1) Manner — how something happens: quickly, gently, loudly, carefully, beautifully. (2) Time — when something happens: yesterday, soon, now, later, always. (3) Place — where something happens: here, outside, upstairs, everywhere, nearby. (4) Frequency — how often something happens: always, often, rarely, sometimes, never. (5) Degree — to what extent: very, completely, almost, quite, extremely.

title: Adverb Forms: With and Without -ly
content: Most adverbs are formed by adding -ly to an adjective: slow → slowly, happy → happily, clear → clearly, careful → carefully, quick → quickly. However, some adverbs do not end in -ly: fast (manner), well (manner), soon (time), here (place), very (degree). Important: not all words ending in -ly are adverbs — 'friendly' is an adjective. Focus on what the word does in the sentence.

title: Adverb Phrases
content: Adverb phrases act like a single adverb but use multiple words: 'in the morning' (time) — 'I exercise in the morning.' / 'with great care' (manner) — 'Handle it with great care.' / 'to a large extent' (degree) — 'The plan succeeded to a large extent.' / 'once in a while' (frequency) — 'We visit once in a while.' / 'in the garden' (place) — 'Children play in the garden.'

title: The Royal Order of Adverbs
content: When using multiple adverbs, English follows this order: Manner → Place → Time. Example: 'He worked hard (manner) in the office (place) yesterday (time).' Placing them out of order sounds unnatural. Frequency adverbs (always, often, never) usually go before the main verb: 'She always arrives on time.'

title: Identify the Adverbs
question_text: Identify the adverbs in: 'She quickly ran outside yesterday.'
explanation: 'Quickly' (manner), 'outside' (place), and 'yesterday' (time) are all adverbs modifying the verb 'ran'.

title: Adverb Type
question_text: What type of adverb is 'very' in 'The movie was very exciting'?
explanation: 'Very' is a degree adverb that intensifies the adjective 'exciting'.

title: Royal Order of Adverbs
question_text: Put these adverbs in the correct Royal Order: 'last week', 'carefully', 'in the garden'.
options: carefully in the garden last week
in the garden carefully last week
last week carefully in the garden
answer: carefully in the garden last week
explanation: Royal Order: Manner (carefully) → Place (in the garden) → Time (last week).

title: Identify Multiple Adverbs
question_text: Which words are adverbs in: 'He always speaks extremely clearly here.'?

title: What Does the Adverb Modify?
question_text: What does the adverb 'beautifully' modify in: 'She sings beautifully'?
explanation: 'Beautifully' is an adverb of manner that modifies the verb 'sings', describing HOW she sings.

title: Correct Adverb Usage
options: He worked hardly yesterday in the office.
He worked hard yesterday in the office.
He worked hardly in the office yesterday.
answer: He worked hard yesterday in the office.
explanation: 'Hard' (not 'hardly') is the correct adverb for effort. The order follows: Manner → Time → Place.

title: Adverb Types in Context
question_text: In 'Tomorrow, we will carefully review the documents', what types of adverbs are used?
explanation: 'Tomorrow' is a time adverb and 'carefully' is a manner adverb.

title: Identify Adverb Phrases
question_text: Which of these are adverb phrases?
explanation: These are adverb phrases. 'Very quickly' contains adverbs but 'very' modifies 'quickly' — it is not a phrase on its own.
